questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of an Expression With the Tangent Trigonometric Function
questions.worked_solution:
We know that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)={sec}^{2}⁡x.$ Applying this formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =1-{sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =1-{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1-(\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Derivative of an Expression With the Tangent Trigonometric Function

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Combinations Given Using Alternate Notation
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that $(\frac{12}{3})$ means the same thing as ${}_{12}{C}_{3}.$

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=12$ and $r=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{12}{C}_{3} & =\frac{12!}{(12-3)!3!} \\  & =\frac{12!}{9!3!} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10\cdot \cancel{9!}}{\cancel{9!}\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 11\cdot 10}{6} \\  & =220.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Evaluating Combinations Given Using Alternate Notation

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+c.$ What is the value of $c?$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=3.$ Therefore, $c=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes When the Denominator Has Complex Roots
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+7x} \\  & =\frac{3}{x({x}^{2}+x+7)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

$$
x({x}^{2}+x+7)=0.
$$

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

- Solving $x=0$ gives the solution $x=0.$

- The equation ${x}^{2}+x+7=0$ has no real solutions because the discriminant $D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={1}^{2}-4(1)(7) \\  & =1-28 \\  & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is $x=0.$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes When the Denominator Has Complex Roots

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980518/assets/ee92f92a52d8ade2052a62a5c19906cd86027b47f22ec986a740b9379e66d8d1.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{1}{8},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{1}{8}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{8}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{8}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{8})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{64}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{63}{64}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{7}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{8}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{3\sqrt{7}}{8})}{(\frac{1}{8})}=3\sqrt{7}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Polynomial Raised to a Power Using the Chain Rule
questions.problem: Given that $f(x)={(5-3x)}^{4},$ find the equation of the tangent at point $(2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f={g}^{4},\,g=5-3x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4{g}^{3},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

Multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4{g}^{3}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-12(5-3x)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at the point where $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & =-12{(5-3(2))}^{3} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(2,1)$ is $m=12.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =12(x-2) \\ y-1 & =12x-24 \\ y & =12x-23\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Differentiating a Polynomial Raised to a Power Using the Chain Rule

Which of the graphs above correspond to an invertible function?
questions.worked_solution:
A function is invertible if and only if it's a one-to-one function. To determine which of the functions are one-to-one, we use the horizontal line test.

From the above, we see that in each of the four given graphs, some horizontal lines intersect the curve more than once. Therefore, these are not one-to-one functions. As a result, none of them correspond to an invertible function.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting Two Exponents
questions.problem: Find the value of $d$ that satisfies the equation ${9}^{d-4}={243}^{d+3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $9={3}^{2}$ and $243={3}^{5}$ as follows:

$$
{({3}^{2})}^{d-4}={({3}^{5})}^{d+3}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2(d-4)}={3}^{5(d+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(3)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $d:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(d-4) & =5(d+3) \\ 2d-8 & =5d+15 \\ -3d & =23 \\ d & =-\frac{23}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting Two Exponents

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral
questions.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{0}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[2{e}^{(k\operatorname{ln}⁡2)/n}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}].$
questions.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=0.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}=\frac{b-0}{n}\,⟹\,b=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{k}=\frac{k\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=2{e}^{{x}_{k}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[2{e}^{(k\operatorname{ln}⁡2)/n}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=2{e}^{x}$ and $b=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

provenance.kp_title: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Factored Polynomial Shown in a Graph
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980518/assets/5e350d9b4db36831eac3ff0708a2acbc903c07265d4c6709632fb8a854121747.png)

Which of the following could be the equation of the polynomial curve shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that the function has precisely three distinct roots, $x=-1$, $x=2$ and $x=5.$

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots:

- Since the graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=-1,$ this root is also a simple root (the multiplicity equals $1$).

- Since the graph passes through $x=2,$ this root has odd multiplicity, and since the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=2,$ the multiplicity must be greater than one.

- Since the graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=5,$ this root is also a simple root (the multiplicity equals $1$).

From the given options, the only possible equation is $y=(x+1)(x-2)^{5}(x-5).$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying the Factored Polynomial Shown in a Graph
